title: AI vs a therapist for relationship help: what each is good for
summary: AI or a therapist for relationship help? An honest look at what each is actually good for, when you need a person, and how to use both.
body_markdown:
Short answer: a therapist is better at the things that need a person, and AI is better at the things that need to happen at eleven at night. They are not really competing for the same job, even though most of the internet frames it as a cage match.


If you are searching this, you are usually in one of two spots. Either therapy is not available to you right now (the cost, the waitlist, a partner who will not go), or you already have a therapist and something keeps going wrong in the six days between appointments. Those are different problems, and they have different answers. So it is worth being specific about[what an app can and cannot do in place of couples therapy](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/is-ai-couples-therapy-any-good) .


## What a therapist can do that software cannot


This part goes first, because it is the part people skip.


- **Hold the room when it gets bad.** A trained person notices the exact moment one of you goes quiet and stops being in the conversation, and can slow things down before it turns into another fight you have to recover from. That live read of two human beings in real time is not something a chat window gives you.
- **Stay with you, and stay accountable.** They remember what you said in March. They push back when you get comfortable. They can name the thing you have been circling for a year and then make you sit in it, which is uncomfortable in a way that works.
- **Treat what is underneath.** Depression, trauma, addiction, an anxiety disorder bending everything else out of shape. Those need assessment and care from a clinician, not reflection.
- **Handle danger.** If there is fear, control, or violence in the relationship, you need a person, and you need one trained for it.


If any of those describe your situation, this is not a close call. Find the person.


## What AI is genuinely good at


- **Being there at the actual moment.** Fights do not schedule themselves for Tuesday at four. They happen after dinner, in the car on the way home, at midnight when the thing is still ringing in your head and your options are wake your partner up or scroll.
- **Costing you nothing socially.** You can say the ugly first draft out loud. *I think I resent her.* *I do not know if I still want this.* You are not managing anyone's face while you say it, and you are not going to hurt someone by thinking out loud.
- **Repetition without embarrassment.** You can go back over the same fifteen minutes of an argument four times in a week. Nobody sighs. Sometimes four times is genuinely what it takes for the shape of it to come clear.
- **Getting you specific before you speak.** Most of what goes wrong in a hard conversation is that the person raising it has not worked out what they are actually asking for. AI is good at this, because it will keep asking until the vague thing turns into a sentence you could say out loud.
- **Getting both of you involved.** A partner who will not book a counselor will often sit through twenty minutes at the kitchen table. That is a lower bar, and lower bars get cleared.


## The six days between sessions


Here is the pattern we run into constantly in Maia conversations, and it is the thing the versus framing misses completely.


A lot of people who show up are already in therapy. They are not looking for a replacement. They had a session on Monday, it was good, they left with something genuinely useful. Then Thursday happened, and by Friday they cannot remember what the useful thing was. What they bring is small and specific: help me work out what just happened in the kitchen, so that on Monday I have something real to say instead of "we had a rough week."


The other version is just as common. Someone two months into a waitlist, using the wait to figure out what they would even say if they got in the room. Both of those are the same underlying job, and it is not the therapist's job. It is the sorting-out that has to happen before and after the hour.


## A reasonable division of labor


Take the live, high-stakes, clinical work to a person. Take the between-times work to the app: the untangling, the rehearsing, the what-am-I-actually-angry-about, the replay of a conversation that went sideways and you still cannot say why.


A concrete version. You have the money fight on Saturday, the one you have had four times. Sunday, instead of re-litigating it or both pretending it did not happen, you spend twenty minutes on it. Alone, using Reflect with Maia, or together, using Heal Together, where you record the conversation and get a read on it afterward that neither of you had to write. What comes out is the actual disagreement underneath the receipts (he thinks you spend without telling him, you think he audits you). Monday in session, you skip the catching-up and start there.


That is not therapy getting replaced. That is therapy getting a better use of its hour. It is also, quietly, how you stop having[the same argument over and over](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-keep-having-the-same-argument) : not by winning it, but by finally getting under it somewhere calm.


## When the honest answer is neither


Some things are not a tools problem.


If your partner will not acknowledge there is anything to work on, no amount of insight on your side moves it. You can get clearer, better prepared, less reactive, and still be the only one in the room doing it. At some point the question stops being which kind of help to get and becomes whether they are willing to do anything at all, which is a harder question and a fairer one. It is worth[being realistic about what any of this can actually change](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/tech-love-how-ai-is-changing-the-game-in-relationship-care) .


And if you are afraid of your partner, if you are being monitored, controlled, or hurt, skip all of this. That is not a communication problem and it does not need better technique. Tell someone you trust, or call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 (US), free and open 24 hours.


For everyone else, you do not really have to settle the debate before you do anything. Bring the thing that actually happened this week. The fight you are still turning over, the sentence you cannot work out how to say. Talk it through with Maia at whatever hour you have it, and if what comes out the other side is "I need to find someone to sit down with," that is a good outcome too.
